label: Curves In R3
notes: Open by explaining that Chapter 5 changes the curve story from bending in a preferred plane to bending with a moving normal plane. The lecture keeps the focus on what can be measured: curvature, torsion, total torsion, binormal motion, and the extra twist carried by a framed curve.

label: Lecture Route
notes: Use the route slide as a contract for the audience. Each topic has a geometric object, a measurable signal, and a diagnostic check. The important shift is that a space curve can bend without choosing a unique normal direction, so frame choices become part of the mathematical data.

label: Unit-Speed Data
notes: Begin from the cleanest setting, a unit-speed curve. The tangent has unit length, so its derivative is automatically normal to the tangent. Curvature measures the size of that normal change, while the normal direction itself is now a moving choice rather than a fixed rotation by ninety degrees.

label: Frenet Frame
notes: Present the Frenet frame as a convenient moving coordinate system when curvature is nonzero. The equations show that curvature couples tangent to normal, and torsion couples normal to binormal. The picture should help students see torsion as rotation of the osculating plane along the curve.

label: Frenet Limitations
notes: The Frenet frame is powerful but fragile. If curvature becomes very small, the principal normal is poorly conditioned, and a numerical trace can flip directions dramatically. This is why the previous chapter's parallel normal fields matter: they separate geometric bending from avoidable frame spin.

label: Torsion Signal
notes: Define torsion as the rate at which the binormal rotates toward the normal direction. A helix makes the signal visible because both curvature and torsion are constant. The warning is that torsion belongs to the chosen Frenet frame, so its interpretation depends on the frame remaining well defined.

label: Total Torsion
notes: Move from local torsion to total torsion by integrating the signal along arclength. The holonomy meter emphasizes accumulation: small rotations of the normal plane can add up to a detectable angle. For closed or nearly closed framed data, the accumulated angle is often more important than a pointwise spike.

label: Tangent Path On The Sphere
notes: The tangent map sends a space curve to the unit sphere. This converts bending of the original curve into a spherical trajectory, and it is a useful way to read elastic space curves. Curvature controls the speed of the tangent path, while torsion describes how the accompanying normal frame turns around it.

label: Elastic Space Curves
notes: Connect the chapter back to the variational theme of the course. Bending energy still penalizes curvature squared, but the curve can now store geometry in torsion and frame rotation. The tangent-sphere view helps separate the energy of changing direction from the choice of normal-plane gauge.

label: Binormal Flow
notes: Introduce binormal flow as a geometric evolution law rather than a fluid-mechanics detour. The velocity is perpendicular to both tangent and normal, so the curve moves through its own binormal direction. The notebook check about small arclength drift is exactly the right diagnostic for a short numerical step.

label: Framed Curves
notes: A framed curve carries a chosen normal director in addition to the centerline. This extra director is not redundant; it records twist that the centerline alone cannot see. The key distinction is between bending of the centerline and rotation of material markings around that centerline.

label: Twist Energy
notes: Frame strain decomposes into bending components and twist components. The twist energy is nonnegative because it is a squared rotational rate, but it can change when the chosen director changes. This slide should make students inspect which quantity is intrinsic to the curve and which belongs to the framing.

label: Example Gallery
notes: Use the examples as a diagnostic dictionary. A planar curve has zero Frenet torsion where the frame is regular, a circular helix has constant curvature and torsion, and a framed circle can have nonzero twist even though the centerline is planar. These examples separate curve geometry from frame geometry.

label: Notebook Diagnostics
notes: Make the computational checks explicit. The notebook asks whether torsion angles are unwrapped consistently, whether moving frames remain orthonormal, whether binormal-flow steps preserve arclength approximately, and whether twist energy stays nonnegative. These are not cosmetic tests; they protect the meaning of the diagrams.

label: Takeaways
notes: Close by tying the chapter to the larger course arc. Space curves force a distinction between the shape of the centerline and the rotation of a normal frame. Curvature, torsion, total torsion, binormal flow, and twist energy are different answers to the same question: what geometric data survives when the picture is moved in space?
